accuracy.evidence: Checked against Gathercole and Alloway (2008): young children hold only a few items in working memory and verbal rehearsal helps keep them; Harvard Center on the Developing Child (2014) names hiding and matching games for ages 3-5 as working-memory practice; Development Matters (2021) Characteristics of Effective Learning for the framing. The lesson claims only that a good look and naming the place help, never that memory is perfect, and treats a wrong lift as normal.

misconceptions.evidence: Predictions target the quick peek, vague words (over there) and leaving things anywhere; lab replies and challenge feedback name each slip: looking away, guessing, under a cup when there are four, mixing up two toys, giving up after an empty cup, dropping things in a new place each day.

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is a set of hiding games built for spatial memory: cups that lift and drop, a one-blink peek round, a speech bubble for the place words, a 3-2-1 count with two toys, a room with a Look again button that briefly shows where things were, and homes found the next day. It only works for remembering where things are.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers by doing: the one-blink peek round is hard and the next rounds with a long look are easy; the count step only works if both places are said; Look again shows the room for a moment to check; the step texts (look, say, check, same home) confirm after the action.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong options: a quick peek (the peek round then shows it is easy to forget), over there (the four-cup round shows which cup is needed), and wherever I left them (the next-day find shows the same home is easiest).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Eight challenge questions, each wrong option tagged with its own slip (away, guess, vague, which, quit, both, peek, homeq); for example Under a cup gets the reply Which cup? There are four. Say its colour too.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses very short sentences and everyday words (look, say, check, cup, under, door) and passes the kid readability limit in validate_lessons; the adult text explains working memory and visual-spatial memory in plain words with named sources.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph gives one action (look, say, check, same home); adult paragraphs give the curriculum link, the evidence for saying it aloud, the common mistakes and what the lab does, with no repeated template text.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark themes: cups and homes fill the width, tray tiles stack in one column at 46 px tall, the speech bubble and count fit above the cups, every button is full width and nothing is clipped at 390 px.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button in the tray (Quick peek, Hide the cups, Lift the red cup, Say: Under the red cup, Pick the shoes, Put it by the door, Look again, Look in the shoe rack); cups carry a white star, dot, triangle or square as well as colour; the canvas aria-label is updated with each reply; walk.cjs reports axe clean in both themes on desktop and phone with every Show me task completing.
